name: Paracetamol (acetaminophen)
summary: The best illustration of why a safety margin can be about a pathway rather than a dose. Paracetamol itself is gentle. A small fraction of it is turned into something that is not, and the body has a limited supply of the thing that neutralises it.
mechanism: Not fully settled even now. Likely central COX inhibition plus an active metabolite, AM404, acting on cannabinoid and TRPV1 systems. It relieves pain and fever but, unlike ibuprofen, has almost no peripheral anti-inflammatory action.

oral.note: Absorption is limited by how fast the stomach empties, not by the intestine. Bioavailability rises with dose, from about 63% at 500 mg to near 90% at higher doses, because the first-pass conjugation pathways begin to saturate.

oral_liquid.note: A solution skips disintegration and dissolution, so it peaks roughly twice as fast as a tablet.

iv.note: Hospital route. Complete and immediate, with no first pass at all.

pathways.name: Glucuronide
pathways.note: The main route. Safe, water-soluble, straight out through the kidneys.

pathways.name: Sulfate
pathways.note: The second safe route. It saturates earlier than glucuronidation, so its share falls as the dose rises — and the overflow goes to the pathway below.

pathways.name: NAPQI (via CYP2E1)
pathways.note: Highly reactive. At normal doses, glutathione in the liver neutralises it as fast as it appears. Glutathione stores are finite: once they fall to roughly 30% of normal, free NAPQI starts binding to liver proteins and killing hepatocytes. This is why overdose damage appears after a delay of a day or more, and why the antidote (acetylcysteine) works by restoring glutathione rather than removing the drug.

chronic_alcohol.note: A double problem: regular drinking induces CYP2E1, sending more paracetamol down the NAPQI route, while poor nutrition depletes the glutathione that neutralises it. This is the best-documented interaction in this set, and the reason the safe dose is lower for heavy drinkers.

fasting.note: Glutathione synthesis needs cysteine from dietary protein; prolonged fasting lowers reserves.

liver_disease.note: Conjugation capacity falls with hepatic function.

child.note: Children rely more on sulfation and have proportionally more glutathione, which makes them somewhat less vulnerable per kilogram than adults.

glutathione.note: A simplified reserve model for teaching the shape of the problem — real glutathione turnover is more complex and varies between people. It is here to show why the danger is a rate problem, not to judge any actual exposure.
